newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds rally on weak jobs data; dollar mixed.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds rally on weak jobs data; dollar mixed.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks and bonds rallied Friday on news of a surprisingly weak U.S. jobs market, but the dollar ended mixed after soaring to the highest levels against the German mark and Japanese yen in years.
The Dow Jones industrial average closed up 82.74 points, or 1.22 percent, at 6,855.80 after an early run-up of more than 95 points.
The rally put the blue-chip index within striking distance of its record closing high of 6,883.90 set on Jan. 21. For the week, the Dow rose 42.71 points.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks and the New York Stock Exchange Composite index both closed at record highs.
In the broader market, advances beat declines 1,627 to 930 on active volume of 538 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Sparking the rally was the employment report for January that showed stronger-than-expected job growth but only slight wage increases. The data muted concerns of wage-driven inflation and eased fears of interest rate tightening any time soon by the Federal Reserve.

Non-farm payrolls rose 271,000 compared with a revised 261,000 the previous month. But analysts said the number had been inflated due to seasonal factors. More importantly, average hourly earnings rose by a mere 1 cent after a sharper rise over the previous two months.
The tame inflation implications of the report sent bonds higher and stocks quickly followed suit.
In the bond market, the bellwether 30-year Treasury bond was up 23/32, or $7.19 on a $1,000 bond, lowering its yield to 6.70 percent from 6.76 percent on Thursday.
"The market got what it wanted, particularly from the hourly earnings number which was very encouraging on inflation," said Guy Truicko, portfolio manager at Unity Management.
The ferocity of the move suggested to analysts that some of January's mutual fund inflows may still be sitting on the sidelines, waiting for an opportunity to enter the market.
"What I see is a lot of cash waiting in the background," said Peggy Farley, chief executive at Amas Securities. "Every time we've seen good news, the market has shot up."
But recently, with every step higher, the stock market has also exhibited increasing wariness.
That skittishness was most apparent during the session's frenzied afternoon, which saw dollar-related comments by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin send markets gyrating wildly.
Rubin signalled that he would not be unhappy with some weakening of the dollar, but he stopped well short of advocating a decline in the U.S. currency.
His comments, however, led speculators to dump greenbacks.
The dollar, which rose earlier to a four-year high of 124.72 yen, slumped to 123 yen from 123.75 on Thursday.
In late trading, the dollar trimmed its gains from a 32-month peak of 1.6755 marks to 1.6582 marks, still above 1.6535 late Thursday.

Gold prices fell to three-year lows on more talk of central bank sales of gold and producer sales. April gold at the new York Mercantile Exchange's Comex division ended down $1.10 an ounce at $344, after posting a new contract low at $339.40.
Crude oil prices fell, ending down $2 a barrel for the week amid slack demand for heating oil and gasoline.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, March gasoline slid a sharp 2.24 cents to 63.06 cents a gallon and March heating oil fell 0.92 cent to 60.53 cents a gallon. March crude oil ended 87 cents a barrel lower at $22.23 a barrel.

At the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee futures ended with gains but off new life-of-contract highs set during the day. March coffee closed at 151.05 cents a pound, up 0.25 cent, after setting a 17-month high at 154.75 cents early.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index closed 41.9 points higher at 4,307.8, up 32 points since the start of the week. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average ended down 171.39 points at 17,867.04 a fall of 462.97 from last Friday's close.
